title: SummitPoint VPC onramp assessment
summary: Initial technical intake to understand SummitPoint's networking constraints for Redwood Private. Key topics: private endpoints vs peering, cross-account peering, region restrictions, Direct Connect/ExpressRoute considerations, KMS/HSM for keys, and audit/logging requirements. Agreed next steps: customer to send VPC diagrams and route tables; Redwood to share security pack and draft pilot plan including regional mapping and cost outline.
topics: VPC peering vs Private Endpoint options
action_items: Marcus: send Redwood Private security pack + SOC2 evidence by 2026-12-13
Sofia: draft pilot network checklist and required route table entries by 2026-12-14
Jared: share current VPC diagram, CIDR ranges, and route tables by 2026-12-12
next_steps: Customer to provide VPC diagrams, route tables, and current peering/transit design
Redwood to propose minimal pilot config (1 region, private endpoints + NAT-less egress pattern) and estimate ramp cost
Schedule a 60-min deep-dive with networking + security SEs next week (calendar invite from Marcus)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Marcus Patel (Redwood AE); Sofia Nguyen (Redwood SE); Jared Li (SummitPoint Infra Lead); Priya Shah (SummitPoint Cloud Architect); Derek Morales (SummitPoint Security Engineer)

[00:00] Marcus: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call — I'm Marcus, AE for Redwood Inference, and Sofia's our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:22] Jared: Morning. Jared here — thanks. We kicked off this to figure out the "onramp" for private connectivity, mostly network, region limits, and security.
[00:34] Priya: Hi, Priya. We're trying to avoid public egress for model calls — data residency in eu-west and us-east is a hard ask for some workloads.
[00:46] Sofia: Got it. We'll walk through options — Private Endpoints (like AWS PrivateLink) vs VPC peering/transit gateway, tradeoffs for cross-account, multi-region, and egress. Quick question up front: do you have a single AWS account for infra or mult-accounts with shared services?
[01:05] Jared: Multi-account. We use a transit gateway in prod, central networking account. We do have Direct Connect to our colo in us-east and ExpressRoute to Azure for some workloads.
[01:18] Derek: Security side: we need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM, keys managed with our KMS and optionally an HSM for model encryption keys, and SAML SSO for the control plane. SOC2 is required.
[01:33] Marcus: Great — that aligns with what we see. Redwood Private supports a customer-managed VPC peering or private endpoints depending on preference; we also do a private control plane pattern for some customers. There are a few nuances — should I sketch the topologies?
[01:50] Priya: Please. Diagrams help.
[02:00] Sofia: (screen share note) So option A: cross-account VPC peering or TGW attachment — low latency, straightforward routing, but you have to manage route table propagation and CIDR overlap. Option B: Private endpoints / PrivateLink — we terminate connections into our customer VPCs via endpoints, less route table work, but you pay for endpoint per AZ and there are sometimes MTU/path MTU issues with some appliances.
[02:29] Jared: For us, avoiding NAT egress is a requirement — we want all traffic over private links and no public IPs. Can Redwood be configured with no outbound public egress?
[02:42] Sofia: Yes, we can operate entirely over private connectivity. For example, we can provision PrivateLink endpoints in your VPC and our service NICs will live in an endpoint network. Alternatively, you can attach our nodes to your TGW — that requires cross-account attachments. Both support no-public-egress patterns, but the operational model differs.
[03:05] Derek: On the KMS/HSM front — does Redwood touch customer keys or do we keep them in our KMS? We prefer customer-managed keys and HSM attestations.
[03:17] Marcus: You keep keys in your KMS. We integrate with customer KMS for disk encryption and can configure envelope encryption where the model artifacts are encrypted with customer keys. For HSMs, we support signing/attestation flows; we'll need to walk through the specific KMS provider (AWS KMS vs Azure KeyVault vs external HSM).
[03:34] Priya: Good. Also latency: some of our inference is latency-sensitive (200ms SLO for p99). How does the regional placement affect that?
[03:46] Sofia: Region matters. If you put workers in eu-west-1 and traffic originates in eu-west-1, you'll be fine. For multi-region failover we can route by policy. The main concern is cross-region KV cache sync — we recommend keeping the serving region local to the traffic for p99 targets.
[04:10] Jared: We're also worried about cross-account peering and route table bloat — we run lots of micro VPCs. Does Redwood support a shared services model (like a single networking VPC with endpoint attachments)?
[04:23] Sofia: Absolutely. We can attach endpoints into your central networking account and then route via TGW to spoke accounts. That reduces the number of peerings. Some customers prefer per-account endpoints for isolation. It's a tradeoff of manageability vs isolation.
[04:40] Priya: One tricky piece is our egress inspection appliance — it changes MTU. You mentioned MTU issues with PrivateLink. Any practical mitigations?
[04:51] Sofia: Often it's a path MTU between your appliance and the endpoint ENIs. We recommend enabling TCP MSS clamping on the appliance or matching MTU on ENIs. If we attach via TGW, MTU tends to be more stable.
[05:07] Derek: Audit logs — we need request-level logging for model invocations and model version metadata for compliance. Can we ship logs to our S3 or SIEM?
[05:18] Marcus: Yes — Redwood Console can forward per-request logs to an S3 bucket (customer-owned) or to a syslog collector via Kinesis/Firehose. For highly sensitive logs you can opt to redact content and keep metadata only. We'll share options in the security pack.
[05:40] Jared: About regional constraints — we need data for eu-west to stay in eu-west for certain customers. Can Redwood pin model serving to region only?
[05:52] Sofia: Yes. You can pin models and traffic policies to a region. We also support failover region for DR, but that requires policy-level consent and potentially changes to data residency which must be documented.
[06:06] Priya: Network ACLs — any specific ports we must open for private endpoints or peering?
[06:14] Sofia: Typically we need TLS (443) outbound to the endpoints, and some control plane ports between your management VPC and our control plane if you choose the private control plane option. We'll give an exact list — it's usually a small set.
[06:29] Marcus: Quick pause — is the preference to have Redwood-hosted model artifacts in your VPC or stored in Redwood storage with encryption keys from your KMS?
[06:39] Derek: Ideally artifacts encrypted with our KMS but stored on Redwood storage accessible over private links. We don't want model weights to land on public buckets.
[06:50] Sofia: That's fine — we can mount S3-compatible storage via private endpoint. We'll also support customer-controlled storage in their account if that's preferred, though lifecycle management for updates gets more complex.
[07:05] Jared: Pricing concern — endpoints per AZ costs add up. For large scale, is peering cheaper?
[07:13] Marcus: It depends on throughput and number of regions. Endpoint per AZ has fixed costs but simpler security posture; peering/TGW has bandwidth costs and management overhead. For steady high-throughput workloads, dedicated attachments can be more cost-effective. We'll include a back-of-envelope in the pilot cost outline.
[07:35] Priya: On the traffic encryption side, TLS is fine but we want mTLS for mutual auth between our apps and Redwood nodes. Supported?
[07:43] Sofia: Yes, we can do mTLS. We'll need to exchange certs or integrate with your PKI. That is part of the onboarding checklist.
[07:58] Derek: A couple of gotchas — auditability in multi-tenant environments. We need assurance that tenant separation holds and that logs show tenant ids for every request.
[08:09] Marcus: Tenant tagging is standard — every request includes a tenant id and model version in metadata. We'll share sample logs.
[08:18] Jared: How about private control plane — what data flows back to Redwood-managed services? We're okay with control plane metadata but not payloads.
[08:28] Sofia: We can do a private control plane inside your network (connect via a private endpoint) so control plane traffic doesn't traverse public internet. Alternatively, you can have a hybrid: control plane in Redwood but with strict audit and no model payloads persisted. We'll outline the differences in the security doc.
[08:47] Priya: For compliance, we need an SOC2 report and penetration test summary.
[08:53] Marcus: We'll send SOC2 Type II and a redacted pentest summary in the pack. Also, we have an attestation for encryption in transit and at rest.
[09:05] Derek: On key rotation — if we rotate KMS keys, do model artifacts need re-encryption or do you support envelope keys so rotation is seamless?
[09:16] Sofia: With envelope encryption, you can rotate the data key without re-encrypting the whole blob; we'll integrate with your KMS for key wrapping. We'll document the exact flow.
[09:30] Jared: Network failover: if eu-west has outage, can we fail to us-east fast? We want deterministic failover for critical customers but aware it affects residency.
[09:41] Sofia: We support policy-based routing. Failover is possible but must be part of the compliance signoff if data residency is enforced. For low-latency SLOs, DR in another region will increase p99.
[09:56] Marcus: Let's capture high-level pilot scope — propose: single region (eu-west-1) pilot, PrivateLink endpoints in central networking account, KMS integration with envelope encryption, mTLS, logs to customer S3, and a small dedicated worker pool to validate latency. Thoughts?
[10:15] Priya: Sounds good. Add one canary app traffic generator so we can measure p50/p95/p99.
[10:22] Sofia: We'll include a synthetic load generator and a short-run perf sheet.
[10:28] Jared: A couple of details on routing — we use BGP over Direct Connect for some prefixes. If we place endpoints in the central network account, will the prefixes be advertised?
[10:39] Sofia: Endpoints themselves don't advertise prefixes; if you need on-prem to reach Redwood nodes without hairpinning, we can work via Transit Gateway attachments that are announced over DX. We'll need to map the exact path.
[10:55] Derek: Any special IAM or role assumptions? We want least privilege and cross-account role for provisioning.
[11:03] Marcus: We use cross-account IAM roles for things that require provisioning into customer accounts. Otherwise, API keys scoped to projects and RBAC via SSO for human access. We'll document permission templates.
[11:18] Priya: What's the expected ops model during pilot — do you provide an SRE contact for infra issues?
[11:25] Marcus: Yes — for pilots we include an SE lead (Sofia) and a named SRE on call for the run. After pilot, if you go to Dedicated, you'd get SLA-backed SRE/ops support.
[11:37] Jared: Regarding model updates — if we pin model versions, how do rollouts work? We want canary with fallback if accuracy regresses.
[11:46] Sofia: Redwood supports canary rollouts per route/model; you can define traffic splits, automatic rollback on error thresholds, and shadowing. We'll share docs and examples.
[11:59] Derek: Anything else about networking gotchas? E.g., port exhaustion or ephemeral ports?
[12:07] Sofia: If you have many short-lived connections, consider keepalive and connection pooling at the app layer — we also support gRPC long-lived streams which reduces ephemeral port usage.
[12:21] Marcus: Time check — we've been going about 12 minutes. Want to open it up for specific topology questions?
[12:28] Jared: Yeah, one specific: we have overlapping CIDR ranges among some test VPCs. That breaks peering. What's the remediation path?
[12:36] Sofia: Overlapping CIDRs push you toward PrivateLink or a NAT-based egress into a shared service VPC that handles translation; we can also suggest SNAT solutions. PrivateLink avoids the overlap because it uses ENIs and endpoint-specific traffic.
[12:55] Priya: For PrivateLink, do we need ENIs in each AZ?
[12:59] Sofia: Usually yes — endpoints are per-AZ. That gives AZ-level redundancy. You'll pay per endpoint and per GB processed.
[13:09] Jared: Are there limits on connections per ENI? We run many concurrent clients in peak.
[13:16] Sofia: We'll provide our tested connection counts; for very high concurrency we recommend a pooling layer or multiple endpoints across AZs.
[13:26] Derek: On SIEM ingestion, can we include raw request headers or do you route only structured metadata?
[13:34] Marcus: We can export both, but for PI or PII we recommend redaction rules. We'll include a sample forwarder config for Kinesis Firehose to S3 to your SIEM.
[13:48] Priya: A non-network question — do you support private model registries or do we rely on Redwood catalog?
[13:55] Sofia: You can bring your own weights and register models in your account; Redwood also provides a model catalog. For private deployment, many customers bring regulated models and control artifact storage.
[14:08] Jared: One last infrastructure item — metrics and tracing. We need distributed tracing across our stack into our APM. Can Redwood emit traces with trace ids?
[14:16] Sofia: Yes — we emit trace context and you can ingest into Datadog/Lightstep/Jaeger using our tracing hooks.
[14:26] Marcus: Alright let's recap and make sure we captured next steps. But before that any more blockers on network that would stop pilot?
[14:35] Priya: CIDR overlap is a blocker unless we do PrivateLink. Also want confirmation on KMS/HSM integration timelines.
[14:43] Derek: SOC2 and pentest deliverables are gating for our security review, but they don't block pilot if we sign an NDA and get the data flows mapped.
[14:56] Marcus: Good — action items we'll capture.
[15:02] [Wrap-up recap begins]
[15:05] Marcus: Recap: Redwood to send security pack, SOC2 docs, pentest summary, and sample route/port checklist. Sofia to draft pilot network checklist and perf plan including synthetic load. Customer to send VPC diagrams, CIDR ranges, route tables, and define one workload to pilot. We'll schedule a 60-min deep-dive next week for network AND security SEs.
[15:30] Jared: Sounds good, appreciate it. We'll aim to get the diagrams and route tables by Sunday (2026-12-12).
[15:39] Priya: We'll also annotate which tenants require strict eu-west residency.
[15:44] Derek: I'll follow up with SIEM ingestion examples we need.
[15:48] Marcus: Great. I'll send calendar invite and the security pack. Thanks everyone.
[15:55] End of meeting.

Notes on transcription quality: some proper nouns (ENI, TGW) were captured correctly; minor mistranscriptions present ("PrivateLink" sometimes appears as "private link"). Speaker labels are accurate though Fireflies sometimes merges speakers.
